title: Limits — Concept and Introduction
notes: A function f assigns a unique element of Y to each element of X. If f(a) is a finite number, f(x) exists at x = a; otherwise it is undefined.
Example: f(x) = 3x + 5 exists at x = 2 since f(2) = 11 (finite). But f(x) = 1/(x−1) is undefined at x = 1 (1/0).
The limit describes the value a function approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a point — even if the function is undefined there.
Geometric interpretation: the y-value the graph is heading toward as x approaches a from either side.
Physical interpretation: instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.
Indeterminate forms (0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0) require special techniques — direct substitution alone is insufficient.
Key standard limits: lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x = 0, lim(x→0) tan(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (e^x − 1)/x = 1, lim(x→0) ln(1+x)/x = 1.
Algebraic properties of limits: lim[f±g] = lim f ± lim g, lim[c·f] = c·lim f, lim[f·g] = lim f · lim g, lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g (denominator ≠ 0).
The Core Philosophy of Limits

A limit asks: as x gets infinitely close to a number, what value is the function heading toward? Sometimes the function has a 'hole' at that exact spot — plugging the number in directly gives 0/0, called an Indeterminate Form. This does not mean the limit doesn't exist; it means the answer is hidden and needs algebra or calculus to expose it. Think of Direct Substitution as checking the front door: if it's unlocked (gives a real number), you walk right in. If it's locked with a 0/0 sign, you need the right tool to pick the lock.
Tool 1 — Direct Substitution (The Front Door)
When to use: always try this first, for smooth continuous functions. Example: lim(x→2) (3x² − 5x + 1) = 3(2)² − 5(2) + 1 = 3.
Tool 2 — Factoring Method (The Common Factor Cleaner)
When to use: if direct substitution gives 0/0 and you see polynomial expressions that share a common factor. Example: lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim(x→3) (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = lim(x→3) (x+3) = 6.
Tool 3 — Conjugate Multiplication (The Radical Vaporizer)
When to use: if you get 0/0 and see a square root expression like √A − B. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (flip the sign): (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B².
Tool 4 — Standard Trigonometric Limits (The Squeeze Anchors)
When to use: for sin(x) or tan(x) ratios approaching zero. The key rule: lim(θ→0) sin(θ)/θ = 1.
Tool 5 — L'Hôpital's Rule (The Nuclear Option)
When to use: if you get 0/0 or ∞/∞ and know derivatives. Differentiate the top and bottom separately (not using the quotient rule), then re-evaluate: lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f'(x)/g'(x).
confusion: Do not confuse limit with function value — f(a) may not exist while lim(x→a) f(x) does.
0/0 is NOT zero — it is indeterminate and requires further analysis.
Left-hand limit and right-hand limit must both exist and be equal for the limit to exist.

universalFacts: Limits are the foundation of all calculus — derivatives and integrals are defined as limits.
Every polynomial, rational, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic function has a well-defined limit at every point in its domain.
The concept of limit bridges algebra and geometry — it allows us to talk about instantaneous rates of change.
This concept is fundamental and appears in multiple contexts across the subject.
Understanding the derivation helps more than memorizing the final formula.
